_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Zuza ma’akha: a coin whose image had been worn away.
rashi:a1.2: And it was not accepted from him: that is, it was not taken in the city for spending; the dinar was not of equal worth to him, it was worth nothing.
rashi:a2.1: Why do I need this further: this “and all of them [are in the shekel of the Sanctuary]”? He already taught it [in the first clause].
gershom:a2.1: Why do I need this further: that he goes back and teaches “and all of them are in the shekel of the Sanctuary, by the Tyrian maneh.”
rashi:a3.1: It was necessary because of the rapist and the defamer: to teach this “and all of them are in the shekel of the Sanctuary,” because the first clause did not say “shekel of the Sanctuary.” For all the others it is obvious to us that they are sela coins, since for the redemption of the son it is written “five shekels apiece by the head” (Numbers 3:47); for the slave it is written “he shall give to his master thirty shekels” (Exodus 21:32); and for the seducer it is written “he shall weigh out silver” (Exodus 22:16). But for the rapist and the defamer “shekel” is not written. One might have thought that when the first clause taught “by the Tyrian maneh,” it meant each one according to its own law: where shekels are written he gives Tyrian shekels, and where shekels are not written he gives Tyrian dinars. The latter clause, “and all of them are in the shekel of the Sanctuary,” teaches us that they are derived from one another, a fixed sum of silver from a fixed sum of silver, as Rav Asi said above. Some books read here: “Are they all things that are redeemed?” That challenges the mishna, which uses the term “redemption” for all of them when it teaches “and all of them are redeemed,” although the term redemption fits only the firstborn. [The answer:] Teach: “All that are redeemed are redeemed with money or with money’s worth,” all that are redeemed meaning, for example, a human firstborn, consecrated property and tithe. Second tithe is redeemed only with minted silver and not with money’s worth; and even minted perutot are fine.
gershom:a3.1: Are these things that are redeemed? The thirty of a slave, and those of the rapist, the seducer and the defamer: what redemption is there in them? [This is the variant reading Rashi mentions.]
rashi:a4.1: And the appearance: to buy the burnt offering of appearance, which is bought with two silver ma’a, as we say in Ḥagiga (2a): “The appearance offering is two silver [ma’a].” These two silver coins must be minted ones.
gershom:a4.1: Teach: All that are redeemed, such as a firstborn and consecrated property, [are redeemed] either with money or with money’s worth, except for the shekels, which are not redeemed with money’s worth.
rashi:a5.1: One combines shekels into darbonot: the townspeople who send their shekels to Jerusalem combine them and buy darbonot with them. Darbonot are minted gold coins: darbonot, yes, but other gold that is not minted, no. In tractate Shekalim (2:1) the reason is explained: lest the pearls drop in value, etc. The same applies to any item of money’s worth: it might drop in value and the Temple treasury would lose; but a coin does not drop in value.
gershom:a5.1: One combines shekels into darkonot: on the first of Adar they announce about the shekels. The treasurer may exchange the shekels for gold darkonot (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss).
gershom:a6.1: Because of the burden of the journey: for one must bring it up to Jerusalem, to the chamber. The reason is the burden of the journey; otherwise, one would redeem only with silver.
rashi:a6.1: And bind up [vetzarta] the money: something that has a form [tzura] on it.
rashi:a6.2: This is the reading: “And the appearance: Rav Yosef [also] teaches: that one should not bring a lump [sigah],” silver dross, but only a minted coin. This baraita of Rav Yosef comes not to explain but to support. [Rashi’s reading adds “also”; the printed Gemara and the Davidson English read without it.]
tosafot:a6.1: And the appearance, Rav Yosef teaches, etc.: Rashi explains that the reading is “Rav Yosef also teaches that one should not bring a lump,” silver dross, but only minted coin, and that this baraita of Rav Yosef comes not to explain but to support. That does not seem right. Why would one need to bring a baraita to support a baraita? Moreover, it should then have said “one does not bring,” not “that one should not bring.” Moreover, it implies, like the others, that a reason is given for each one. So it seems that it does come to explain, giving a different reason: were he to bring money’s worth, he would sometimes bring a lump or dross silver that is not worth two silver ma’a, and they would not sell him a good burnt offering of appearance for that lump as they would if he had brought minted silver.
gershom:a7.1: The appearance: which is a silver ma’a. He cannot bring money’s worth, only refined silver.
gershom:a8.1: Rav Yosef teaches: that one should not bring a sigah to the courtyard: dross silver mixed with other metals.
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. One does not redeem [a human firstborn] with slaves, etc.: even though we said above (49b) that one redeems with money or with money’s worth.
rashi:a7.2: Nor with notes: if he holds a note against his fellow for five sela coins and gives it to the priest so that the priest will collect that debt as the redemption of his son, the son is not redeemed.
rashi:a7.3: Nor with consecrated items: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a7.4: He wrote to the priest that he owes him five sela coins: for the redemption of his son.
rashi:a7.5: And his son is not redeemed: as we say in the Gemara, lest people say that one redeems with notes.
rashi:a7.6: Therefore: since we said that he is obligated to give him five sela coins, if the priest wishes to give them back to him as a gift, he may. But there is no other remedy.
tosafot:a7.1: He wrote to the priest that he owes him five sela coins: In Ketubot, at the beginning of HaNosei (102a), this is cited in connection with the dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish over “I owe you a maneh” written in a document. Rashi explains there: for example, where he wrote it to him in a document and gave it to him before witnesses, and they disagree whether it counts as an admission, since the matter is strengthened by being in a document even though he did not say to them “You are my witnesses.” Rabbeinu Tam explains: for example, where he came to obligate himself through that document even though he owed him nothing. The whole passage there must be explained accordingly, and I explained it there.
gershom:a9.1: One does not redeem the firstborn with slaves or with notes: he cannot give the priest a note of debt that he holds against others for the redemption of his son.
gershom:a10.1: He wrote to the priest, etc., and his son is not redeemed: until he gives.
gershom:a11.1: Therefore: since it is the priest’s money, if the priest wishes to give him, as a gift, the five sela coins he received from him, he may.
rashi:a8.1: Shall be yours, and you shall surely redeem: when the redemption is yours, then he will be redeemed. The Merciful One said this verse to Aaron.
rashi:a10.1: Gemara. It restricted: to silver, and not to anything else.
rashi:a11.1: It restricted notes: since they are not worth anything.
rashi:a12.1: “You shall redeem”: it generalized again. Even though this “you shall redeem” is written before the detail, we nevertheless treat it as a generalization and a detail, as we say below.
rashi:a13.1: Which are compared to land: “And you shall bequeath them [to your children after you]” (Leviticus 25:46).
rashi:a15.1: Hasol (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a16.1: And we say: in tractate Kiddushin (21a).
rashi:a16.2: On what do they disagree? Rabbi expounds generalizations and details: “and you shall take” is a generalization, “awl” is a detail, “and you shall put it through his ear” generalizes again. Just as the detail is explicitly of metal, so too anything of metal.
rashi:a16.3: And Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda expounds it with amplifications and restrictions: what did it amplify? It amplified everything. And what did it restrict? It restricted a drug [sam, a caustic substance].
rashi:a17.1: Here: this is the reason he expounds amplifications and restrictions, as the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught at the end of Elu Terefot (Ḥullin 67a): wherever it says “in the water,” “in the water” twice, that is, wherever two generalizations are stated next to each other with a detail after them. For example here: “This you may eat of all that is in the water: whatever has fins and scales in the water.” These are two generalizations, implying that in all waters we require fins and scales. And a detail is written after them, “in the seas and in the streams,” implying that in seas and streams, which flow, we require fins and scales, but fish that grow in collected waters may be eaten without fins and scales. This is not a generalization and a detail; we do not treat it as a generalization and a detail, but rather place the detail between them and treat it with amplifications and restrictions [so Rashi’s text reads]. So here too: “and its redemption from one month” is a generalization, “you shall redeem” generalizes again. These are two generalizations next to each other with the detail after them, and therefore we expound them with amplifications and restrictions.
rashi:a19.1: And the Rabbis: who expound them with generalizations and details, hold as we say in the West.
gershom:a12.1: Rabbi expounds generalizations and details: “and you shall take” is a generalization, any kind of taking; “awl” is a detail; “and you shall put” generalizes again. With a generalization, a detail and a generalization, you may include only what is similar to the detail: just as the detail is of metal [so too anything of metal]. And Rabbi Yosei expounds “it amplified, restricted and amplified”: it amplified everything.
gershom:a13.1: Yes, generally Rabbi expounds generalizations and details; and here, with the firstborn, what is the reason he expounds amplifications and restrictions? Because in “and its redemption from one month you shall redeem,” two generalizations are written next to each other, and then a detail, “by your valuation, silver.” It is like what the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: “in the water,” “in the water,” twice, as it is written: “This you may eat of all that is in the water: all that has fins and scales in the water,” and afterward the detail is written, “in the seas and in the streams.” Since the generalizations are written next to each other, this is not a generalization and a detail but rather “it amplified and restricted.”
gershom:a14.1: And the Rabbis, who expound generalizations and details with the firstborn: Ravina said, they hold as they say in the West: “Wherever,” etc. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text gives this answer in Ravina’s name; the printed Gemara reads “And the Rabbis say.”]
tosafot:a20.1: Say: nor may consecrated items be redeemed with any of these: In Pesaḥim (35b) and in HaZahav (Bava Metzia 54a) it is cited, regarding consecrated property that one redeemed onto land, that it is not redeemed, since it is written: “And he shall give the money and it shall be established as his.” That implies they expound it from that verse. But one cannot say so, since in Torat Kohanim, on the portion Beḥukotai, it is expounded from “And every valuation of yours shall be by the shekel of the Sanctuary,” as Rashi explains there. There [in Pesaḥim and Bava Metzia] the Gemara did not bother to cite more than one of the verses about consecrated property in which “money” is written. So we find in several places that it does not cite the main exposition in every place: as it cites in Kiddushin (3b) “in her youth, in her father’s house,” that all the gain of youth belongs to her father, even though that is written about the annulment of vows; and likewise in Gittin (21b), “a scroll” cuts her off and nothing else cuts her off, an exposition that the Rabbis do not hold, only Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
rashi:b1.1: Nor are consecrated items redeemed with any of these: with slaves, notes and land. There we derive it from verses in Torat Kohanim, in the portion of valuations.
gershom:b1.1: Say: nor are consecrated items redeemed with any of these, with slaves, land and notes, because “money” is written of consecrated property, as it is written: “And he shall give the money and it shall be established as his.”
rashi:b2.1: Lest they say one redeems with notes: even without giving anything; or else, with a note he holds against his fellow.
tosafot:b2.1: Ulla said: by Torah law his son is redeemed when he gives: At first glance it is implied at the beginning of HaNosei (Ketubot 101b) that Ulla’s view holds only according to Reish Lakish. But one can reconcile it so that it holds even according to Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:b3.1: His son is redeemed when he gives: for he has given the redemption.
tosafot:b3.1: But the Rabbis say his son is not redeemed: This is puzzling, since the mishna too teaches “he is obligated to give him, and his son is not redeemed.” One can deflect this: [the mishna] means he is not redeemed until he gives him the money, and the mishna comes to teach that even if he converted the five sela coins into a loan owed to the priest, it is not as though the priest had received them and lent them back to him; and if the priest waived them, the son is not redeemed until he gives.
rashi:b4.1: All at once: he placed five sela coins before all of them and went away.
rashi:b4.2: One after the other: [part to one priest] and then to another priest after that; so it is taught in the Tosefta. He has fulfilled his obligation.
rashi:b4.3: He took them: the priest took them and returned them to him; he has fulfilled his obligation.
gershom:b2.1: We learn this: in the mishna, that if the priest wishes to give it to him, he may, as the baraita teaches, “he took them and returned them to him,” he may. Evidently that is the halakha, that he may.
gershom:b3.1: He gave the five sela coins to ten priests, half a sela to each, all at once: he has fulfilled his obligation, since he gave all five sela coins.
rashi:b5.1: Rabbi Tarfon: he was a priest.
gershom:b5.1: He fulfilled even this halakha: for he showed everyone that the halakha is so, that one may return it.
rashi:b6.1: Rabbi Ḥanina: he was a priest.
rashi:b6.2: Would go and sit before him: so that Rabbi Ḥanina would see him walking and coming before him, and would return to him the five sela coins he had given for his son. [Rashi’s text reads “would go and sit before him”; the printed Gemara reads “was going and coming before him.”]
rashi:b6.3: He said to him: You did not conclusively give: a complete giving, but only so that I would return them to you.
rashi:b6.4: You did a bad thing: therefore your son is not redeemed if I return them. Another explanation: even if I do not return them, your son is not redeemed.
tosafot:b6.1: He said to him: You did not conclusively give; you did a bad thing [midaam bish]: One can explain midaam as “anything,” since we render me’uma [anything] in Aramaic as midaam; that is, you did not conclusively give anything. One can also explain “midaam bish you did” as “you did a bad thing,” since “a bad thing” is rendered in Aramaic “kol midaam bish” (II Kings 4). And there are books in which “you did” is not written, only “midaam bish” and nothing more, that is, it is a bad thing, a bad business.
tosafot:b6.2: Therefore his son is not redeemed: This is puzzling: how is this different from a gift on condition that it be returned, where we say in the first chapter of Kiddushin (6b) that his son is redeemed, since it concludes that in all of these cases he acquires? One can answer that here Rabbi Ḥanina wished to acquire only as a complete gift, because there [in Kiddushin] doing so is forbidden, since he looks like a priest who helps at the threshing floors, as we derived above in chapter Ad Kama (26b), because it says: “You have corrupted the covenant of Levi.” And even though the man gave it to him without saying anything, it is as though he had explicitly said “on condition that he return it to me,” since there was a clear sign of the matter; and this is not a case of words in the heart, as with “he sold and did not need the money” in chapter Almana (Ketubot 97a). It is still somewhat puzzling: since Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Ḥanina would return it all the time, they turn out to corrupt the covenant of Levi, for other priests would lose, since people would give only to them, because they were accustomed to return it. One can answer that the giver does not know at the time of giving whether it will be returned to him, so “you have corrupted the covenant of Levi” does not apply, for what does it matter to us what he returns to him afterward? Also, perhaps they returned it only to the poor, and not to people like themselves, the rich.
gershom:b6.1: He saw that man: who had given five sela coins to Rabbi Ḥanina, [who] was a priest.
gershom:b7.1: And that man was going and coming: that is, he wanted Rabbi Ḥanina to return them to him.
gershom:b8.1: He said to him: Rabbi Ḥanina said, I see in your mind that you did not resolve in your mind to give me anything except on condition that I return them to you. Therefore, if I return them to you, your son is not redeemed, and I may not return them to you, since you did not resolve in your mind that they be mine. Rather, I will seize them, and your son will be redeemed.
gershom:b9.1: One who designates the redemption of his son and it was lost before it reached the priest’s hand bears responsibility for it, as it is said: “of man and of animal shall be yours, but you shall surely redeem,” etc. That is: when will it be yours? At the time when you surely redeem, from hand to hand.
gershom:b10.1: From where do we derive this: that he bears responsibility for it.
rashi:b7.1: From where do we derive this: that he bears responsibility for it. And even though the mishna cites a verse, he asks “From where do we derive it?”, and below Rav Pappa challenges him on this.
rashi:b7.2: It is derived from “valuation,” “valuation”: it is written here, of the firstborn (Numbers 18:15–16): “And its redemption from one month you shall redeem, by your valuation.” Just as with valuations one bears responsibility for them until they reach the hand of the treasurer, as it says in the last chapter of Shechitat Ḥullin (139a): “And he shall give your valuation on that day” (Leviticus 27:23): they are non-sacred in your hand until they reach the hand of the treasurer.
gershom:b11.1: It is derived from “valuation” and “valuation,” from valuations: here it is written “and its redemption from one month you shall redeem, by your valuation,” and “your valuation” is written of valuations. Just as with valuations, when he says “My valuation is upon me,” he bears responsibility for it, so too with the firstborn he bears responsibility for it.
rashi:b8.1: Just as with the burnt offering of appearance one bears responsibility for it: for it is an obligation upon him, which is no less than a vow, where if the animal died or was stolen he bears responsibility for it, since it is as though he carries it on his shoulder. Moreover, it is written: “And none shall appear before Me empty” (Exodus 23:15); if it died or was stolen and he did not replace it, he would turn out to have appeared empty in the courtyard. But from the “none shall appear” of the firstborn we would not have learned this, since that does not mean a literal appearance: he does not bring it to the courtyard but gives it to the priest, and I would have said that designating it is enough.
gershom:b12.1: Just as with the burnt offering of appearance one bears responsibility for it: even though he set it aside, he bears responsibility for it, since he cannot come to the courtyard if he does not bring one. So too with the redemption, he bears responsibility for it.
rashi:b9.1: A verse for a verse? Need he bring a verse to support a verse? The tanna of the mishna cited another verse for it.
gershom:b13.1: A verse for a verse: that is, since we learn it in the mishna from the verse “shall be yours, but you shall surely redeem,” why do Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan need to learn it from another verse? [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text names Rabbi Yoḥanan where the printed Gemara has Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yonatan.]
rashi:b10.1: From where do we derive this: that he is obligated to give after the death.
rashi:b10.2: “Valuation,” “valuation,” from valuations: as it says in tractate Arakhin (20a): if he said “My valuation is upon me” and died, the heirs must give; if he said “So-and-so’s valuation is upon me” and that person died, the one who vowed must give. It is derived from a verse (in tractate Arakhin), and in Torat Kohanim: “One might think that if he said ‘So-and-so’s valuation is upon me’ and that person died, he would be exempt; the verse states ‘he shall value him,’ even if he died.” So too here, when the son died after thirty days, the father had already become obligated in his redemption.
gershom:b14.1: It is derived from “valuation” and “valuation,” from valuations: just as there the heirs are obligated, as we learned in tractate Arakhin, “One who says ‘So-and-so’s valuation is upon me’: if the one who vowed died, the heirs must give,” so too here with the firstborn, where he died after thirty days, the heirs are obligated to give.
rashi:b11.1: Just as: with the burnt offering of appearance the heirs are obligated, since it is an obligatory burnt offering, so too here, when the son died after thirty days, the father had become obligated in his redemption. And of an obligatory burnt offering we learned: a woman who brought her sin offering and died, the heirs bring her burnt offering.
rashi:b11.2: So too here the heirs are obligated: after the death of the father and the son, when the obligation had already taken effect and they then died.
gershom:b15.1: Just as there: with the burnt offering, the heirs are obligated, as we learned: a woman who brought her sin offering and died, the heirs bring her burnt offering. So too here the heirs are obligated.
rashi:b12.1: Mishna. In the property of the mother: her melog property [property she brought into the marriage, which her husband enjoys but does not own].
rashi:b12.2: In the enhancement: if the property increased in value after the father’s death, before they divided it, the firstborn does not take a double portion of the enhancement. Rather, they assess what it was worth at the time of their father’s death, and the firstborn, who took two portions of the land, pays money for the value of the enhancement of the second portion he took on account of the birthright, and that money is divided among all of them.
rashi:b12.3: In property due: property of which their father did not have possession at the time of his death, but which was due to fall to him as an inheritance and fell to them later. The firstborn does not take a double portion in it.
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: In Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 125b) the halakha is that the firstborn takes no double portion in a loan owed to the father, whether the heirs collected money or not, which would suggest that a widow too cannot collect her marriage contract from such a loan, since the mishna says she has no share in property due. But Ri explains that a loan, though counted as “due” for the firstborn, counts as “possessed” for a widow’s marriage contract, as the mishna in HaKotev (Ketubot 84a) shows: Rabbi Akiva gives a loan or deposit held by others to the heirs only because the widow and the creditor need an oath and the heirs do not, and no one there disagrees. Tosafot reject the reading that this follows Rabbi Meir alone, since, as Rabbeinu Tam explains, even Rabbi Meir lets a marriage contract be collected only from the yavam’s movables, not from orphans’ movables (Ketubot 80b–81b; Kiddushin 65b); and the same mishna gives a creditor the same right, which no tanna gives from orphans’ movables. So the reason must be that the loan was never in the orphans’ hands. Neither Rabbi Meir’s nor Rabbi Natan’s “two stringencies” apply (Ketubot 82a), and the same holds for detached produce held by others. Now that the Geonim enacted that widows and creditors collect from orphans’ movables, a widow collects even from a loan owed to her husband, whether the orphans collected land or money; Tosafot answer the objection that this adds a second stringency (the Geonim treated movables fully like land; and for Rabbeinu Tam, who holds the enactment is Torah law, there is no stringency at all). The practice is to let women collect from their husbands’ loans. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b16.1: And he does not take a double portion in the enhancement by which the property increased after his father’s death.
gershom:b17.1: Nor in property due as in property possessed: if his father’s brother died without sons after his father’s death, then, since his father was due to inherit his brother but died first and did not have possession of his brother’s property, the firstborn does not take a double portion in it.
